lifeline

Medics rush a wounded soldier to a waiting helicopter in a swirl of blue, in a painting of 1967 by Ronald A. Wilson, a US Army combat artist in Vietnam. Medical evacuation helicopters saved thousands of lives.
starlight
Ronald A. Wilson painted this night scene in purple shades in 1967, as a US Army combat artist. The name refers to the starlight scopes that helped soldiers see in the dark.
mortar-attack-counterfire
Flares light up the night sky while glowing lines of tracer fire cross the dark in this blue painting of 1967 by Ronald A. Wilson. It shows a night when a base answered a mortar attack.
down-trail
A swirling, almost abstract picture of a trail through the jungle in Vietnam by James Pollock in 1967. He was one of the Army's combat artists, who were sent to record the war in their own style.
get-them-out
Soldiers in dark, heavy shapes struggle in a tense scene by Stephen H. Randall from 1968. The US Army combat artists painted both the action and the feelings of the war.
emmeline-pankhurst-arrested-outside-buckingham-palace

Police carry the British suffragette leader Emmeline Pankhurst away on May 21, 1914, after she tried to bring a petition to King George V at Buckingham Palace. She was arrested many times for the cause of women's votes.
nellie-mcclung
Nellie McClung, the Canadian writer and activist who led the campaign that made Manitoba the first province to give women the vote in 1916. This portrait is from about 1910.
leaders-of-the-women-s-social-and-political-union-about

Women's Social and Political Union leaders meet around 1906. Founded by Emmeline Pankhurst in 1903 with the motto 'Deeds, not words,' the WSPU used marches and protests to demand votes for women in Britain.
millicent-fawcett-and-louisa-garrett-anderson

Millicent Fawcett, the leader of Britain's peaceful suffrage societies, sits with her niece Louisa Garrett Anderson. Fawcett believed in persuading Parliament by law-abiding campaigns, and she led the movement for decades.
saint-charlemagne-karel-veliky
Master Theodoric, the court painter to Emperor Charles IV in Prague, painted Charlemagne as a saint in the 1360s. Charles IV, who was named for Charlemagne, admired his great predecessor.
